stem: Siringo calls himself an 'old stove up cow puncher' and writes that his excuse for writing is money. What does that tell a historian about his book as a source?

stimulus.source_note: Charles A. Siringo, A Texas Cow Boy (1885), title page and Preface. Public domain. Text verified against Project Gutenberg (eBook #38309).
stimulus.text:
Charles A. Siringo, A Texas Cow Boy (1885), title page and Preface (ellipses mark omissions):

Title page: AN OLD STOVE UP "COW PUNCHER," WHO HAS SPENT NEARLY TWENTY YEARS ON THE GREAT WESTERN CATTLE RANGES

Preface: "My excuse for writing this book is money—and lots of it." ...

"While ranching on the Indian Territory line, close to Caldwell, Kansas, in the winter of '82 and '83, we boys, there being nine of us, made an iron-clad rule that whoever was heard swearing or caught picking grey backs off and throwing them on the floor without first killing them, should pay a fine of ten cents for each and every offense. The proceeds to be used for buying choice literature, something that would have a tendency to raise us above the average cow-puncher. ... There being two young Texans present who could neither read nor write, we let them speak their choice after the rest of us got our votes deposited. At the word given them to cut loose they both yelled 'Police Gazette', and on asking why they voted for that wicked Sheet, they both replied as though with one voice: 'Cause we can read the pictures.'"

options.text: It is useless, because Siringo admits he wrote only for money
options.misconception: Background: a source written for money can still be useful; historians weigh motive, they do not discard a witness for having one.

options.text: It is a firsthand account by a working cowboy, written to sell
It is an official government report on the cattle industry
options.misconception: Background: Siringo was a cowboy writing his own life, not a government official reporting on the industry.

options.text: It proves the dime novels were accurate histories
options.misconception: Background: Siringo's book is a memoir, not a verdict on the dime novels, which romanticized the West he lived in.

rationales.A: Background: a source written for money can still be useful. Historians weigh motive, they do not discard a witness for having one.
rationales.B: Siringo lived the life he describes, twenty years on the ranges, so he knows the work from inside. But he says plainly he wrote for money, so a historian reads his tales as a showman's memories, not as sworn testimony.
rationales.C: Background: Siringo was a cowboy writing his own life, not a government official reporting on the industry.
rationales.D: Background: Siringo's book is a memoir, not a verdict on the dime novels, which romanticized the West he lived in.
rationales.general:
Picture a retired cowboy, broke and crippled, deciding to sell his life story.
1. Ask what he knows. Twenty years on the ranges, from the inside, not from a library.
2. Ask why he writes. He says so himself: money, and lots of it.
3. Name the source. A true witness with a reason to entertain, so check his stories against other evidence.
Remember: a witness can be honest and still be selling you something, so believe the work and verify the tales.
